case.case_title: Chandrasiri v. Gen. Cyril Ranatunga and Others

clause.text: Every person has the right to apply to the Supreme Court for violations of fundamental rights.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner's detention under Emergency Regulations was lawful or violated his fundamental rights, and whether he could seek redress under the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that his detention was unlawful and violated his fundamental rights under Articles 13(2) and 13(4) of the Constitution, and sought relief for this violation.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents argued that the detention orders under Regulations 19(2) and 17(1) of the Emergency Regulations were valid and justified based on suspicion of subversive activities and national security concerns.
key_facts: Petitioner was arrested on 19.03.1990 by army officers and detained without a valid detention order initially.
Detention orders under Regulation 19(2) and later Regulation 17(1) were issued but lacked supporting material to justify detention.
Petitioner was detained for over two years and later sent for rehabilitation before release.
Respondents failed to provide investigation reports or intelligence material to justify detention orders.
The petitioner was deprived of employment and sought compensation for unlawful detention.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that the right to apply to the Supreme Court for violations of fundamental rights includes the right to challenge unlawful detention. The Court emphasized the need for material justification for detention orders under Emergency Regulations and that subjective satisfaction of the Secretary must be supported by evidence.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found no material to justify the detention orders under Regulations 19(2) and 17(1). The detention was held unlawful as the respondents failed to produce evidence or intelligence reports. The order for rehabilitation was also invalid as it was based on invalid detention.
principles_established: Detention under Emergency Regulations must be supported by material evidence.
Subjective satisfaction of authority making detention orders must be demonstrable to the Court.
Unlawful detention violates fundamental rights and entitles the detainee to compensation.

outcome.holding: The Court held the detention unlawful and violative of the petitioner's fundamental rights under the Constitution. The petitioner was awarded compensation and costs.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The State was ordered to pay Rs. 50,000 as compensation and Rs. 1,500 as costs to the petitioner.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 17 is central as it grants the petitioner the right to apply to the Supreme Court for violations of fundamental rights, which is the basis for the Court's jurisdiction and consideration of the unlawful detention claim.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court granted leave to proceed with the application for alleged violation of fundamental rights and found the detention invalid and violative of Articles 13(2) and 13(4), ordering compensation.
